notes.2:23: The Greek text reads "Hivites" (for Hebrew "Avvim"), "Asedoth" (for Hebrew "Hazerim"), and "Cappadocians who came out of Cappadocia" (for Hebrew "Caphtorim who came out of Caphtor").
notes.2:25: The Greek uses a second-person imperative ("begin to put") addressed to Israel, whereas the Hebrew has first-person ("I will begin to put"); the phrase "On this day" stands at the end of 2:24 in this Greek text.
notes.2:33: The Greek verb is third-person singular ("He struck down"), making the Lord the subject, whereas the Hebrew reads first-person plural ("we struck down").
notes.3:1: This Greek text reads "Gog" here and in 3:13, while reading "Og" in 3:3, 3:4, 3:10, and 3:11.
notes.3:5: The Greek renders the Hebrew expression for "unwalled villages" as the ethnic name "the Perizzites."
notes.3:9: The Greek reads "the Phoenicians" and "Sanior" where the Hebrew reads "the Sidonians" and "Sirion."
notes.3:14: This Greek text preserves the distinct names "Arbok" (for "Argob"), "Gartasi" and "Homachathi" (for "Geshurites" and "Maachathites"), and "Basemath" (for "Bashan"); similarly, 3:10 transliterates "Misor" (Hebrew "the plain") and 3:17 reads "Machanareth" (Hebrew "from Chinnereth").
notes.3:27: "The Hewn Peak" translates the Greek epithet rendering Hebrew "Pisgah"; likewise, 3:25 specifies "Antilebanon" where the Hebrew reads "Lebanon," and 3:26 reads "disregarded" where the Hebrew reads "was angry with."
notes.4:34: The Greek reads "great visions" (horamasin megalois), reflecting a Hebrew reading related to sight/visions where the Masoretic Text reads "great terrors."
notes.4:43: "Gaddi" (Gaddei) transliterates the Hebrew gentilic for the Gadites, standing in the Greek as a proper name parallel to Reuben and Manasseh.
notes.4:47: The Greek text explicitly reads "Gog" (Gog) here where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Og."
notes.4:48: The Greek text reads "Mount Sihon" (Seon), matching the spelling of king Sihon in verse 46, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Mount Sion."
notes.4:49: "Asedoth the hewn" (Asedoth ten laxeuten) combines a transliteration of Hebrew Ashdoth with a Greek rendering of Pisgah as "the hewn," corresponding to "the slopes of Pisgah" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.5:3: The Greek text uses second-person plural pronouns ("your fathers... with you... you who are all here") in 5:2-3, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses first-person plural ("our God... our fathers... us").
notes.5:14: This Greek witness includes the creation clause ("for in six days the Lord made both heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them"), paralleling Exodus 20:11 alongside the Exodus redemption motive in 5:15.
notes.5:17: The Greek Septuagint places the prohibition against adultery (5:17) before murder (5:18), reversing the Hebrew Masoretic order (cf. Luke 18:20; Romans 13:9).
notes.5:33: The Greek reads "so that He may give you rest" (katapause), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "that you may live."
notes.6:4: The Greek text prefixes an introductory superscription ("And these are the ordinances and the judgments which the Lord commanded the sons of Israel when they went forth from the land of Egypt") before the Shema, absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.6:5: The Greek reads "with all your mind" (dianoia), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "with all your heart" (cf. Matthew 22:37; Mark 12:30).
notes.6:8: Greek asaleuton literally means "immovable" or "unshaken," rendering the rare Hebrew term totaphot ("frontlets" or "phylacteries").
notes.6:16: Greek en to Peirasmo ("at Testing") translates the Hebrew place name Massah ("testing") rather than transliterating it.
notes.6:25: Greek eleemosyne ("mercy" or "charitable righteousness") renders Hebrew tsedaqah ("righteousness"), reflecting a frequent Septuagint equivalence in Deuteronomy.
notes.7:1: The Septuagint lists the Amorite before the Girgashite (whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text places the Girgashite before the Amorite) and reads "great nations" rather than "many nations."
notes.7:16: The Greek reads "all the spoils of the nations" (panta ta skyla ton ethnon), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "all the peoples."
notes.7:21: The Greek verb trothese literally means "be wounded" (rendering Hebrew ta'arots, "dread" or "be terrified"), and describes God as "mighty" (krataios) rather than "awesome."
notes.7:24: The Greek reads "from their place" (ek tou topou ekeinon; compare standard Septuagint ekeinou, "from that place"), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "from under heaven."
notes.8:3: Following the Septuagint, this verse omits "which you did not know," reads "God" rather than the divine name, and explicitly supplies "word" (rhemati) along with the repeated clause "shall man live"—wording closely echoed in Matthew 4:4.
notes.8:4: The Septuagint adds the clause "your sandals did not wear out upon you," reads "your feet did not become calloused" (instead of the Hebrew "your foot did not swell"), and introduces the forty years with "behold."
notes.8:15: The Greek describes the wilderness creature as a "biting serpent" (ophis daknon) rather than the Hebrew "fiery serpent," and specifies "a spring of water" (pegen hydatos) from the flinty rock.
notes.8:17: The Greek noun dynamis (here paired with the Septuagint addition "great") can mean either "power" or "wealth," reflecting Hebrew chayil in the context of material prosperity (vv. 13, 18).
notes.9:4: The Greek text adds "good" ("this good land") and omits the closing clause found in the Hebrew ("rather it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the Lord is driving them out before you").
notes.9:13: The Greek includes "I have spoken to you once and twice, saying," emphasizing the Lord's repeated warnings; this clause is absent from the Hebrew text.
notes.9:22: Rather than transliterating the Hebrew place names (Taberah, Massah, and Kibroth-hattaavah), the Greek translates them by their meanings: "the Burning," "the Testing," and "the Graves of Craving."
notes.9:24: The Greek reads passively, "from the day He became known to you," whereas the Hebrew reads actively, "from the day I knew you."
notes.9:26: The Greek addresses God as "O Lord, King of the gods," corresponding to Hebrew Adonai YHWH.
notes.10:2: The Greek text reads the second-person future "you shall write" (matching Exod 34:27), whereas the Hebrew text reads first-person "I will write" (compare 10:4).
notes.10:3: Greek "incorruptible wood" (literally wood that does not rot) is the standard Septuagint rendering of Hebrew acacia wood.
notes.10:6: The Greek preserves the distinct proper-name forms "Beeroth of the sons of Jakim" and "Misadai," corresponding to Hebrew Beeroth Bene-jaakan and Moserah.
notes.10:7: The Greek preserves the distinct proper-name forms "Gadgad" and "Taibatha," corresponding to Hebrew Gudgodah and Jotbathah.
notes.10:16: The Greek renders the idiom directly as "the hardness of your heart," where the Hebrew reads literally "the foreskin of your heart."
notes.11:16: "be enlarged" translates Greek platynomai ("widen" or "enlarge"), where the Septuagint reads the underlying Hebrew verb as widening rather than being enticed or deceived.
notes.11:18: "unmoved" renders Greek asaleuton ("immovable" or "unshakable"), the Septuagint's distinctive rendering of the Hebrew term traditionally translated "frontlets."
notes.11:24: "Antilebanon" preserves the Septuagint's distinct proper name (Antilibanou), referring to the eastern mountain range, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Lebanon."
notes.11:30: "near the lofty oak" reflects the Septuagint's plesion tes dryos tes hypseles, rendering Hebrew "oaks of Moreh" descriptively; the Greek also transliterates Gilgal as Golgol and locates Canaan "toward the west."
notes.12:3: Following the Septuagint, Israel is commanded to cut down the groves and burn the carved images—reversing the verbs of the Hebrew Masoretic Text—and "their name shall perish" is intransitive.
notes.12:6: The Codex Vaticanus Septuagint text here is shorter than the Hebrew Masoretic Text, listing burnt offerings, freewill offerings (homologias), and the firstborn of herds and flocks; the fuller list appears in 12:11.
notes.12:18: "the sojourner" translates Greek proselytos ("sojourner" or "resident alien"), which stands in the Septuagint here where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the Levite."
notes.12:27: The Septuagint text here is markedly shorter than the Hebrew Masoretic Text, omitting the instructions regarding placing the flesh and pouring the blood upon the altar.
notes.13:1: In the Greek numbering this verse opens chapter thirteen, whereas in the Hebrew Masoretic Text it concludes chapter twelve (12:32), shifting the remaining verses of chapter thirteen by one.
notes.13:7: The Greek text explicitly includes "by your father or" alongside "by your mother," whereas the Hebrew text mentions only "the son of your mother."
notes.13:10: The Greek reads "you shall surely report concerning him" (anangellon anangeleis), reflecting a different verbal reading from the Hebrew "you shall surely kill him."
notes.13:14: Here and in verse sixteen the Greek refers to "their land" and "that land" (ge), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "their city" and "that city."
notes.14:1: The Greek text states only the prohibition against making baldness between the eyes for the dead, without the Hebrew clause forbidding ritual self-laceration.
notes.14:5: The Greek lists five permitted wild animals—including the pygarg (white-rumped antelope) and the giraffe (kamelopardalis)—where the Hebrew text lists seven.
notes.14:13: Verse fourteen of the Hebrew text ("every raven according to its kind") is absent from this Greek witness, so the numbering proceeds directly from verse thirteen to verse fifteen.
notes.14:21: The Greek specifies "a lamb" (arna) rather than the Hebrew "a young goat."
notes.14:26: The Greek omits the list of oxen, sheep, wine, and strong drink, reads "your son" (ho huios sou) rather than "your household," and connects verse twenty-seven directly to the rejoicing without the Hebrew clause "you shall not forsake him."
notes.15:10: The Greek repeats the injunction from verse eight to lend the needy brother as much as he requires according to his lack.
notes.15:18: The Greek reads "the yearly wage of a hired servant" (ephetion misthon), whereas the Hebrew text reads "double the wage of a hired servant."
notes.16:1: The Greek renders Hebrew Abib as "the month of new fruits" (literally "of the new [produce]") and adds "by night" at the end of the verse.
notes.16:7: The Greek reads "boil and roast," harmonizing Exodus 12:8-9 with Deuteronomy, and specifies "your houses" rather than "your tents."
notes.16:8: The Greek adds the closing exception "except whatever shall be done for a soul" (referring to preparing food, as in Exodus 12:16), which is not in the Hebrew Masoretic text.
notes.16:18: The Greek term grammatoeisagōgeis ("recorders") refers to judicial clerks who introduced written records in court, rendering Hebrew shoterim ("officers").
notes.17:7: The Greek reads masculine singular "the evil one" (ton ponēron) rather than abstract "the evil," matching the form quoted in 1 Corinthians 5:13.
notes.17:9: This Greek witness names only "the judge" while keeping plural verbs ("having inquired, they shall declare"), omitting "the Levitical priests" found in the Hebrew text.
notes.17:14: Throughout 17:14-20 the Greek renders Hebrew "king" as "ruler" (archōn) and "kingdom" as "rule" (archē).
notes.17:18: The Greek phrase to deuteronomion touto ("this second law" or "this copy of the law") is the origin of the English title Deuteronomy.
notes.18:5: The Greek adds "to stand before the Lord God" and "to bless," and concludes with "among the sons of Israel" rather than "all the days."
notes.18:10: The Greek renders "make pass through the fire" as "purifies in fire" (perikathairōn) and ends the verse with dative pharmakois ("with spells/potions"), which governs "chants an incantation" in verse 11.
notes.18:11: Greek engastrimythos literally means "ventriloquist" (belly-speaker) and is the Septuagint term for a necromantic spirit-medium.
notes.18:22: The Greek reads "you shall not spare him" (literally "you shall not hold back from him"), whereas the Hebrew text reads "you shall not dread him."
notes.19:4: The Greek idiom 'before yesterday and the third day' (also in 19:6) reflects a Semitic expression meaning 'previously' or 'in time past.'
notes.19:17: The Greek text here reads 'shall know' (gnōsontai, following Codex Vaticanus) rather than 'shall stand' (stēsontai), which appears in other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew.
notes.19:19: The Greek uses the masculine singular 'the wicked one' (ton ponēron), pointing directly to the false witness rather than evil in the abstract.
notes.20:5: Where the Hebrew refers to 'officers,' the Septuagint renders the term as 'scribes' (grammateis) here and in verses 8–9.
notes.20:14: The Greek terms aposkeuē ('dependents' or household retinue) and apartia ('belongings' or movable goods) correspond to 'little ones' and 'livestock' in the Hebrew.
notes.20:15: The Greek text connects 'not from the cities of these nations' directly to the prohibition in verse 16, omitting the repeated introductory clause found in the Hebrew.
notes.20:19: The Greek explicitly reads 'one city' and frames the closing clause as a rhetorical question ('Is the tree in the field a man...?') expecting a negative answer.
notes.21:4: The Septuagint specifies a 'rough ravine' rather than a perennial stream valley, and 'hamstring' (neurokopēsousin, severing the sinews) rather than breaking the heifer's neck as in the Hebrew.
notes.21:12: In verses 12–13 the Greek uses second-person singular verbs ('you shall shave... pare... remove'), assigning these actions to the Israelite man rather than to the captive woman as in the Hebrew.
notes.21:17: The Greek reads 'the beginning of his children' (archē teknōn autou), where the Hebrew has 'the beginning of his strength.'
notes.21:23: The Septuagint explicitly includes 'everyone' (pas) in 'everyone who is hanged upon a tree is accursed by God,' a wording closely echoed in Galatians 3:13.
notes.22:9: The Greek reads "with a double crop" (diphoron) and "be consecrated" (hagiasthē, i.e., forfeited to the sanctuary), rather than the Hebrew "two kinds of seed."
notes.22:21: The Greek uses the masculine singular "the evil one" (ton ponēron, also in verses 22 and 24), the exact Septuagint phrasing later quoted in 1 Corinthians 5:13.
notes.22:29: The Greek specifies "fifty didrachmas of silver," using the Alexandrian two-drachma coin as the equivalent of the shekel.
notes.23:1: In the Septuagint, chapter 23 begins with this verse (22:30 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text), shifting the subsequent verse numbers by one.
notes.23:8: The Greek has Idoumaion ("Idumean"), the Septuagint designation for an Edomite.
notes.23:11: The Greek text here reads "he shall go out into the camp," a notable Codex Vaticanus reading where other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew read "outside the camp, and he shall not enter into the camp."
notes.23:18: The Septuagint preserves a fourfold prohibition, rendering the Hebrew terms both as "harlot" and "fornicator" and as female and male initiates (telesphoros and teliskomenos) of pagan mystery cults.
notes.23:25: In the Septuagint, the laws regarding a neighbor's standing grain (v. 25) and vineyard (v. 26) appear in reverse order from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.24:4: The Greek reads "you shall not defile" (mianeite), differing from the Hebrew "you shall not bring sin upon."
notes.24:10: This Greek text omits the negative particle before "enter," forming a continuous conditional clause leading into the command to stand outside in verse 11 (contrast the Hebrew and some Greek manuscripts, "you shall not enter").
notes.24:13: Greek eleemosyne ("mercy" or "charity") renders the Hebrew term for "righteousness."
notes.24:17: This Greek text ends after "and the widow," omitting the clause about taking a widow's garment in pledge found in the Hebrew and some Greek witnesses, and opens verse 18 directly with "for."
notes.25:1: The Greek uses the neuter "what is right" (to dikaion) in contrast to the masculine "the ungodly man" (tou asebous).
notes.25:2: Greek "you shall seat him before them" (kathieis) differs from the Hebrew "cause him to lie down," and omits the clause about beating him according to the measure of his guilt.
notes.25:6: The Greek reads simply "the child whom she bears" (to paidion), without specifying "the firstborn" as in the Hebrew.
notes.25:15: The Greek includes only the command for a true and just weight, without repeating the parallel clause for a measure found in the Hebrew.
notes.26:5: The Greek uses the third-person verb "he shall say" (erei) and renders the confession "My father forsook Syria" (Syrian apebalen ho pater mou), contrasting with the Hebrew "you shall say" and "a wandering Aramean was my father."
notes.26:8: Greek "with great visions" (en horamasin megalois) reflects a reading of the Hebrew root for "vision" rather than "terror."
notes.26:12: The Greek explicitly specifies "the second tithe" (to deuteron epidekaton) rather than the Hebrew "the year of tithing."
notes.26:17: The Greek translates the covenantal verbs in verses 17 and 18 with "chosen" (heilou and heilato) and reads "God" rather than "the Lord" in verse 17.
notes.27:7: "A sacrifice of deliverance" renders Greek thysian sōtēriou, the Septuagint's standard term for the peace or fellowship offering. The Septuagint also includes the phrase "and be filled" (kai emplēsthēsē), which does not appear in the Masoretic Hebrew text.
notes.27:15: Here and throughout verses 15–26, the Greek text translates the liturgical response with the optative verb Genoito ("So be it") rather than transliterating the Hebrew "Amen."
notes.27:22: The Greek reads "the sister of his father or his mother" (his aunt), differing from the Masoretic Hebrew, which speaks of "his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother."
notes.27:23: The Greek reads "his daughter-in-law" (nymphēs autou) where the Hebrew reads "his mother-in-law," and adds an extra curse concerning a man's wife's sister that is not present in the Masoretic text.
notes.27:26: The Septuagint's wording "every man" (pas anthrōpos) and "in all the words" (en pasin tois logois) is more expansive than the Masoretic Hebrew and aligns closely with the form of the verse cited in Galatians 3:10.
notes.28:4: The Greek text here omits "and the produce of your land" (which appears in 28:18 and in the Hebrew Masoretic Text), listing only offspring, cattle, and sheep.
notes.28:5: Greek apothekai ("storehouses") and enkataleimmata ("reserves" or "what remains," also in 28:17) represent the Septuagint's distinctive rendering of the Hebrew terms commonly translated "basket" and "kneading bowl."
notes.28:7: Throughout the blessings (28:7-13) and curses (28:20-28, 35), the Greek regularly uses optative forms ("May the Lord..."), casting these declarations as solemn liturgical wishes rather than simple future statements.
notes.28:25: The Greek text reads episkopen ("a visitation" or "reckoning," as in Codex Vaticanus), whereas other Greek witnesses read enkopen ("defeat" or "rout").
notes.28:32: Following Codex Vaticanus, the Greek text omits the clause about sons and daughters given to another nation (likely lost through similar endings with 28:31), so neuter plural auta ("them") refers directly back to "your sheep" in 28:31.
notes.28:36: The Greek text reads plural archontas ("your rulers") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has singular "your king."
notes.28:48: Following Codex Vaticanus, the Greek text specifies only "in hunger and in want of all things," without "in thirst and in nakedness" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other Greek witnesses.
notes.28:65: The Greek text reads kardian heteran apeithousan ("another, disobedient heart," as in Codex Vaticanus), whereas other Greek manuscripts read "a despondent heart" and the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "a trembling heart."
notes.28:69: In the Septuagint and Hebrew versification, this summary statement concludes chapter twenty-eight as 28:69; most English Bibles number it as 29:1.
notes.29:7: The Greek reads first-person singular "I gave" (where the Masoretic Text has "we gave") and uses the gentilic transliteration Gaddei ("the Gadites") alongside "Reuben."
notes.29:18: The Septuagint renders the sinner's self-blessing as "May good [literally 'holy/favorable'] things come to me" and interprets the closing clause ethically as "so that the sinner may not destroy the sinless along with himself" (where the Hebrew metaphor speaks of sweeping away the watered with the dry).
notes.29:28: The Greek consistently uses second-person plural pronouns ("your God," "to you and to your children"), whereas the Masoretic Text uses first-person plural ("our God," "to us and to our children").
notes.30:3: The Septuagint distinctively reads "the Lord shall heal your sins," whereas the Masoretic Text speaks of the Lord restoring Israel's captivity or fortunes.
notes.30:6: The Greek verb perikathariei ("shall thoroughly cleanse") renders the Hebrew metaphor of circumcising the heart in an explicitly purifying sense.
notes.30:14: The Septuagint adds "and in your hands" after "in your mouth and in your heart," highlighting practical obedience alongside speech and inner devotion.
notes.30:20: The Greek uses the neuter pronoun touto ("for this is your life"), pointing to loving, heeding, and holding fast to the Lord rather than the personal pronoun "He."
notes.31:1: The Greek text reads 'finished speaking' (syntelesen lalon), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'went and spoke.'
notes.31:6: The Septuagint uniquely includes three verbs of fear ('do not fear, nor be dismayed, nor be terrified') and the doubled phrase 'with you, among you' (meth' hymon en hymin).
notes.31:21: The Greek text omits the opening clause found in the Hebrew ('and when many evils and troubles have come upon them') and renders Hebrew 'inclination' as 'wickedness' (ten ponerian).
notes.31:23: By referring to the Lord in the third person ('which the Lord swore... He Himself'), the Greek text presents Moses rather than the Lord as the speaker commissioning Joshua here.
notes.31:29: The Greek critical text omits a verb before 'evils at the end of the days,' preserving an abrupt elliptical clause found in major Septuagint witnesses such as Codex Vaticanus.
notes.32:8: The Greek reads "according to the number of the angels of God," an important Septuagint reading supported by early Dead Sea Scrolls witnesses, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the sons of Israel."
notes.32:15: "The beloved one" translates Greek ho egapemenos, the Septuagint rendering of the poetic Hebrew title Jeshurun for Israel.
notes.32:35: The Greek reads "In the day of vengeance I will repay," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Vengeance is Mine, and recompense."
notes.32:43: The Septuagint preserves a fuller hymnic conclusion than the Masoretic Text, calling upon the heavens, the sons of God, the nations, and all the angels of God to rejoice and worship Him (cf. Romans 15:10; Hebrews 1:6).
notes.32:49: The Greek reads "in the land of Canaan" for the location of Mount Nebo, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in the land of Moab."
notes.33:2: The Greek text reads "myriads of Kadesh" and "angels with Him," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "ten thousands of holy ones" and "a fiery law for them."
notes.33:5: "The beloved" translates Greek ho egapemenos (also in 33:26), the Septuagint rendering of the poetic Hebrew name Jeshurun.
notes.33:8: Greek "manifestations" and "truth" translate the Hebrew Urim and Thummim, while "Testing" (Peira) and "Contradiction" (Antilogia) translate the place names Massah and Meribah.
notes.33:10: The Greek text reads "in Your wrath continually," reflecting a rendering of Hebrew be'appekha ("in Your nostril/wrath") and taking the following term to mean "continually" rather than "whole burnt offering."
notes.33:19: The Greek text reads "They shall utterly destroy nations," diverging from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("They shall call peoples to the mountain").
notes.34:1: "Araboth of Moab" (also in 34:8) preserves the Greek transliteration of Hebrew araboth, meaning "the plains" or "steppes."
notes.34:6: The Greek uses a plural verb ("they buried him"), transliterates Hebrew "in the valley" as the place name "Gai," and renders Beth-peor literally as "the house of Peor."
notes.34:7: In this Greek text, the final verb ("nor were they impaired") continues with "his eyes" as its subject, without the Masoretic Text's reference to his vigor or other Septuagint witnesses' addition of "his cheeks."
notes.34:9: Standard English "Nun" renders the Septuagint Greek form Naue for the name of Joshua's father.
